name: AI for Customer Service and Communication
objectives: Given your most common customer questions, write an FAQ with AI help, with ten questions and every answer checked against what you really do
Given how you want your business to sound, describe your brand voice and have AI write in it, with three voice words and a do and don't list placed at the start of the chat

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Finding your top customer questions and building an FAQ
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List your most common customer questions and turn them into a checked FAQ.
This lesson builds toward: Given your most common customer questions, you will write an FAQ with AI help, with ten questions and every answer checked against what you really do.
Most businesses answer the same ten questions over and over: hours, prices, parking, delivery, booking, returns, payment types, wait times, allergies or materials, and "do you do...?".
Write them down first from memory, your texts and your messages. Then give an AI assistant your real answers in rough form and ask it to turn them into a clear FAQ: "Here are my rough answers. Make a short FAQ for my nail salon website. Friendly, simple words."
Check every answer against what you really do. An FAQ on your website or on a sign is a promise to customers.
Step by step:
- List the ten questions you hear most.
- Write your real answer to each, roughly.
- Ask AI to turn them into a clear FAQ.
- Check every answer, then post it on your site, social page or counter.
Words to know:
- FAQ: frequently asked questions: a list of common questions and their answers.
Try it now: Write your ten most common customer questions with a rough answer for each. Ask an AI assistant to make a short, friendly FAQ from them, then check every answer.
You can now build a checked FAQ from your real customer questions.

check.q: Why is an FAQ like a promise to customers?
options: Because customers will rely on what it says
Because it is a legal contract
Because it is posted only once
check.why: Customers act on your FAQ, so every answer must be true.

check.q: AI's FAQ says you offer free parking, but you do not. What would you do?
options: Fix the answer to match what you really do
Ask AI to remove all answers
check.why: FAQ answers come from your real policies, checked by you.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Setting your brand voice
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Describe how your business sounds and have AI write in that voice.
This lesson builds toward: Given how you want your business to sound, you will describe your brand voice and have AI write in it, with three voice words and a do and don't list placed at the start of the chat.
Your brand voice is how your business sounds. A family taqueria might be warm and playful; a tax preparer calm and professional; a barbershop relaxed and neighborly.
Pick three words for your voice and write a short do and don't list: "Do: use first names, say thank you, keep it short. Don't: use slang, use all caps, make promises about times."
Give this to the AI at the top of a chat: "Write in this voice for every reply." Now every answer sounds like the same business, no matter who on your team sends it.
Step by step:
- Pick three words for how you want to sound.
- Write three dos and three don'ts.
- Paste them at the start of a chat.
- Ask for a sample reply and check it sounds right.
Words to know:
- Brand voice: the way a business sounds in its messages.
- Consistent: the same each time.
Try it now: Write your three voice words and your dos and don'ts. Paste them into an AI assistant and ask for a reply to "Are you open on Sunday?" Does it sound like you?
You can now describe your brand voice and get AI replies that sound like your business.

options: How your business sounds in messages
check.why: Brand voice is the way your business sounds when it talks to customers.

check.q: You want every AI reply to sound like your bakery. What would you do?
options: Ask for a new tone each time
Use all caps to sound excited
Put your voice words and dos and don'ts at the start of the chat
check.why: Giving AI your voice at the start helps every reply match it.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Reply templates for messages, texts and email
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make reusable reply templates with placeholders.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant, you will create five reusable reply templates with placeholders, in your brand voice, checked and saved where you can copy them quickly.
A reply template is a ready answer with blanks. You fill in the blanks each time, so you answer in seconds without retyping.
Useful templates: booking confirmation, appointment reminder, order ready, running late, sorry we are out of an item, and thank you after a visit. Ask AI: "Using my brand voice, write five short text templates for a mobile car-wash business. Use [customer name], [date] and [time] as blanks."
Keep templates in your phone's notes or text shortcuts, or in your booking tool if it allows saved replies. Never paste real customer names, phone numbers or card details into the AI to make them; use the blanks.
Step by step:
- Pick five situations you reply to often.
- Ask AI for a short template for each, with blanks in brackets.
- Check the wording and facts.
- Save them where you can copy them fast.
Words to know:
- Reply template: a saved answer with blanks you fill in each time.
- Placeholder: a blank like [customer name] that you fill in with real details later.
Try it now: Ask AI for five reply templates in your brand voice with [blanks]. Check them and save them where you can copy them quickly.
You can now make and save reply templates that let you answer customers fast and consistently.

options: A message you reuse with blanks to fill in
check.why: A template is a ready reply with blanks you fill in each time.

check.q: You want a template for "your order is ready". What would you give AI?
options: A real customer's name and phone number
check.why: Blanks keep private details out and make the template reusable.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Reviews, hard conversations and trust

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Answering online reviews, good and bad
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write honest replies to positive and negative reviews, and follow the FTC review rule.
This lesson builds toward: Given a positive or negative online review, you will write an honest, calm reply with AI help, with every statement true and no fake or paid-for reviews.
Customers read how you answer reviews. Thank good reviews by name of the dish or service, briefly. For bad reviews, stay calm: thank them, say sorry for their experience, fix what you can, and invite them to contact you directly. Do not argue in public or share their private details.
AI helps you write a calm reply when you are upset. Paste the review text (not the reviewer's private info) and ask: "Write a short, polite reply. Apologize, mention we have retrained our staff on wait times, and invite them to call us." Only say what is true.
Never write fake reviews, buy them, or use AI to make them. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has a rule, in effect since October 2024, banning fake reviews and testimonials, including AI-made ones, and paying for reviews only if they are positive. Read the FTC's questions and answers page to learn what is allowed.
Step by step:
- Read the review twice and wait if you are angry.
- Ask AI for a short, polite draft.
- Make sure every statement is true.
- Invite unhappy customers to contact you directly.
- Never write, buy or fake reviews.
Words to know:
- Review: a customer's public rating and comment about your business.
- FTC: Federal Trade Commission: the US agency that protects consumers from unfair and deceptive business practices.
- Testimonial: a customer's statement praising a business, used in its marketing.
Official sources:
- FTC: Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule, Questions and Answers
- FTC: Final Rule Banning Fake Reviews and Testimonials (August 2024)
Try it now: Find one real review of your business (or write a sample bad review about a late order). Use AI to draft a calm reply, check every statement is true, and edit it into your voice.
You can now reply to good and bad reviews calmly and honestly, without breaking the FTC's fake review rule.

check.q: Which review practice does the FTC rule ban?
options: Paying customers only if they leave positive reviews
Asking all customers for honest reviews
check.why: Rewarding only positive reviews is banned under the FTC rule.

check.q: A harsh review makes you angry. What would you do?
options: Reply right away in capital letters
Post a fake good review to balance it
Ask friends to argue with the reviewer
Wait, reread it, then write a calm, true reply
check.why: Waiting helps you reply calmly and honestly.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Calming an upset customer
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a simple four-step method, with AI help, to answer an upset customer.
This lesson builds toward: Given an upset customer and your refund and redo limits, you will write a reply using the LAST method, offering only a solution you would really give.
A simple method works for most complaints: Listen, Apologize, Solve, Thank (LAST). Listen to the whole complaint, apologize for the experience, offer a fair solution you can really give, and thank them for telling you.
Decide your limits before you need them: when you give a refund, a redo, a discount or a free item. AI can draft the message, but you choose the solution. Do not let AI promise something you have not agreed to.
If a customer threatens, harasses or mentions injury, safety or legal action, keep the reply short, do not admit fault in writing, and talk to a professional or your insurer.
Step by step:
- Listen: read or hear the whole complaint.
- Apologize for the experience.
- Solve: offer a fair fix within your limits.
- Thank them for telling you.
- Ask AI to draft it, then check the promise is one you will keep.
Words to know:
- LAST: Listen, Apologize, Solve, Thank: a method for complaints.
- Escalate: pass a serious problem to the owner, a professional or an insurer.
Try it now: Write your refund and redo limits in three lines. Then use AI to draft a LAST reply to: "My cake was the wrong flavor and the party is ruined." Check the solution is one you would really give.
You can now answer an upset customer with the LAST method and a fair, real solution.

check.q: What is the first step of the LAST method?
check.why: LAST starts with listening to the customer.

check.q: AI's reply to an upset customer offers a full refund plus free service for a month, more than your limits allow. What would you do?
options: Change it to a fix within your limits
check.why: You choose a fair fix within the limits you set, not the AI.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Privacy, honesty and your customer service kit
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put your service tools together and keep customer data private.
This lesson builds toward: Given your FAQ, templates and replies, you will put together a customer service kit that keeps customer data private, in one document, with every fact checked and no real customer details.
Customers trust you with their names, phone numbers, addresses and sometimes card details. Keep those out of AI tools. Work with placeholders, and fill in the real details yourself in your phone or booking system.
If you use a chatbot on your website or messages, tell customers they are talking to an automated helper and give them a way to reach a person. Review what it says regularly.
Now put it all in one document: your brand voice, your FAQ, your templates, your LAST method with your limits, and your review reply. Share it with your staff so everyone answers the same way.
Step by step:
- Check every template uses placeholders, not real data.
- If you use a chatbot, label it and offer a person.
- Collect voice, FAQ, templates, LAST limits and review replies in one document.
- Share it with your team.
Words to know:
- Chatbot: an automated program that answers messages.
- Customer data: information about your customers, such as names, phone numbers and orders.
Try it now: Final task: put your brand voice, ten-question FAQ, five templates, one upset-customer reply and one review reply into one document. Check every fact and remove any real customer details.
You can now run your customer service with a checked, private, consistent kit made with AI help.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Brand voice No voice words or no do and don't list. Three voice words and a do and don't list. Sample replies clearly match the voice. Checked FAQ Fewer than ten questions, or an answer that is not true. Ten common questions with answers checked against what you really do. Answers are short and in the brand voice. Reply templates Fewer than five, or templates with real customer details. Five checked templates with placeholders. Saved where staff can copy them quickly. Upset customer reply Defensive, or offers a fix you would not give. Follows LAST and offers a fix within your limits. Your refund and redo limits are written in the kit. Review reply Argues, says something untrue, or is missing. Calm, honest and in your voice. Says what you are fixing and invites the customer to contact you. Privacy and facts Real customer details in the kit or the AI chat, or unchecked facts. No customer private data used, and every fact checked. The kit notes how a chatbot, if used, says it is automated and offers a person. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why share your customer service kit with staff?
options: So everyone answers the same way
check.why: A shared kit keeps replies consistent across your team.

check.q: You are making templates and have a real customer's card details in your notes. What would you do?
options: Paste them into the AI so it understands
Use them as an example template
Share them with staff in the kit
Keep them out of the AI tool and the kit
check.why: Customer card details must stay out of AI tools.
